Text and Commentary


I. JUDGMENT ON SAMARIA AND JERUSALEM (1:1–16)


Micah 1 contains three interrelated units: the superscription (1:1), the introduction to the book in the form of a judgment oracle (1:2–7), and a prophetic lament over the Shephelah (1:8–16). The superscription provides the name of the prophet, the kings of Judah under whom the prophet lived, and the theme of the book (the fate of Samaria and Jerusalem). The judgment oracle begins with a call to the nations, but then admonishes Jerusalem to learn a lesson from the fall of Samaria (722 BCE). The prophetic lament proleptically warns villages in the Shephelah that Jerusalem will soon fall, and they will become collateral damage.

The interrelated nature of the three sections provides a level of coherence to the whole. The theme of the book (the fate of Samaria and Jerusalem) in 1:1 anticipates the next unit (1:2–7) which contains the only other reference to Samaria. That reference to Samaria (1:5–7) presumes knowledge of its destruction (722 BCE) and warns Jerusalem that a similar fate awaits her. Similar ideas appear in 1:10–16 with the threat that has reached the gate of Jerusalem (1:9, 12). The pronouncements to the villages in 1:8–16 presuppose some form of 1:2–7 but evoke the impending attacks in the time of Hezekiah (701 BCE) when the Assyrian king solidifies control of the Levant and the coast.

Despite this coherence, a significant number of scholars have argued that the passage is composite, with each unit exhibiting signs that more than one hand helped to shape the final form. Specifically, the king list and the thematic summary have been connected to an exilic redaction that joined Micah with Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah. This combination of kings provides a patterned series of superscriptions, and the thematic summary at the end of 1:1 fashioned the first chapter into a warning to Jerusalem to learn from the overthrow of Samaria. Several scholars suggest that the superscription was expanded in the aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction, and a number of those have associated the expansion with the inclusion of Micah with Hosea and Amos in some way.1

The second unit in Mic 1 comprises 1:2–7. The literary parameters of the unit are seldom challenged.2 Nevertheless, three major issues remain contested: its authorial homogeneity, the unit’s logical flow, and the date of composition. Authorial homogeneity is often assumed rather than analyzed closely.3 The theme of the verses changes dramatically, moving from a call to judgment on the nations (1:2), to a theophany report (1:3–4), and then to an admonishment to Jerusalem not to follow Samaria on its path of idolatry (1:5–7).

Explaining the internal logic of 1:2–7 also creates debate, and explanations of the core passage vary widely. In the history of interpretation of these verses, several portions of 1:2–7 have been suggested as reflecting the interest of later editorial hands because their inherent relationship to the surrounding context is not immediately apparent. The biggest debate about the literary integrity of 1:2–7 centers around 1:2, but several scholars have suggested that 1:3–4 or, more commonly, 1:5–7 (or portions thereof) entered the corpus as insertions that expanded a base text. Hence, individual scholars have concluded that 1:2–7 contain secondary material, and every verse in the “unit” has been claimed as an insertion by someone because it does not flow inherently with the surrounding text because a later editor inserted the verse.4

The date of composition of 1:2–7 continues to defy consensus, with scholars arguing that the core of these verses stems from the eighth century, the seventh century, or the sixth century. Decisions on these issues greatly affect how individual scholars interpret the passage, but these issues intertwine with one another. To illustrate, consider disagreements about the literary relationship of 1:2 to 1:3–7 and the relationship of 1:2–7 to 1:10–16.

The literary development of 1:2–7 over time remains a debated topic, especially because scholars wrestle with the logical relationship of 1:2 to the surrounding verses and the relationship of 1:2–7 (in its entirety) to 1:8–16. A number of scholars have treated 1:2 (or portions of the verse) as a late addition to an existing introduction to chapters 1–3.5 Two factors fuel this claim. First, the syntactical meaning of 1:2 concerns judgment against the nations, while 1:3–7 anticipate judgment against Yahweh’s people. The role of judgment against the nations remains a conundrum, however, since that topic does not appear until Mic 4–5; therefore the thematic relationship between the judgment against the nations in 1:2 and the rest of Micah aligns the verse more closely with chapters 4–5 than with 1:3–7.6 Second, chapters 4–5 are widely considered postexilic expansions to the early material in chapters 1–3, and in this author’s opinion represent the latest block of texts in the book.7 Connecting 1:2 with chapters 4–5 affects opinions about the date of composition of 1:2.

Further, for rhetorical purposes, distinguishing between 1:2–7 and 1:8–16 allows one to focus on the introductory role that the former plays for the book and on the conceptual shift of the latter that ratchets up the danger. Reasons for these distinctions are discussed at the beginning of those units. Nevertheless, 1:8–16 appears to assume some form of 1:2–7, especially because 1:8 refers back to all this.

The final section of Mic 1 consists of 1:8–16. These verses present a dramatic prophetic address to personified cities that proleptically warns both the Shephelah and Jerusalem of Yahweh’s impending judgment. The unit opens with a lament proper (1:8–9), spoken by the prophetic figure. Two sets of warnings ensue after the lament, one warns villages in the Shephelah that they will be destroyed when Jerusalem is punished (1:10–12) and the other treats the recent destruction of Lachish as an ominous warning of the destruction to come (1:13–16), including the prophet’s own hometown (Moresheth-Gath in 1:14). The mention of Lachish, the warning of a military threat, and the movement toward Jerusalem suggest that the passage evokes the events of Sennacherib’s campaign in 701 BCE wherein he destroyed Lachish and laid siege to Jerusalem. This campaign solidified Assyrian control of the coast and provided an unhindered path to Egypt so that within forty years, Assyria would conquer Thebes and control Egypt politically, albeit briefly.





A. SUPERSCRIPTION (1:1)


1The worda of Yahweh which came to Micah, the Moreshite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah;b the word that he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

a. The LXX indicates a vav at the beginning of the superscription (“And the word of the Lord came”). None of the Hebrew or Greek manuscripts from the Judean Desert exhibits this reading. It thus appears to be a later addition or a loose translation.

b. BHK suggests the phrase “in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” was added to Mic 1:1, and points to Hos 1:1 and Amos 1:1. This has source critical and redaction critical implications, but it is not a textual variant. See exegesis of Mic 1:1 below.

This superscription provides four pieces of information: (1) the word event formula identifying the prophetic recipient; (2) the prophet’s hometown; (3) a list of three Judean kings communicating a time frame for Micah’s ministry; and (4) a thematic summary of the prophet’s message. The question of how these four pieces came to be in the superscription deserves consideration in light of the traditions it records and the growth of the book.

1 The word event formula begins the superscription: The word of Yahweh came to. This formula typically introduces a prophetic speech or a prophetic book, and it contains two essential components: the affirmation of divine authority and the identity of the prophetic recipient. The affirmation asserts divine communication has taken place in the form of a message from Yahweh. It asserts Yahweh is the source of the following material. The Hebrew word translated as came in this formula is the verb hyh, a verb that has a wide range of meanings in English: “to be,” “to become,” or “to happen.” It is the same verb from which the Tetragrammaton derives—and the basic idea is one of existence.8 The selection of came picks up on the idea of “happened.” Literally, the formula means that the word of Yahweh “was” to Micah. The Hebrew idiom does not focus upon the mode of reception. The word event formula does not state that Micah “heard” the word of Yahweh or that he “dreamed” or “saw” a vision. More profoundly, it affirms that what follows carries the weight of an encounter with the divine. It conveys Yahweh as the source of what follows and, simultaneously, sanctions Micah as the recipient of the message.

The word event formula names Micah the Moreshite as the prophet to whom the word came. The name Micah follows a pattern of theophoric names that appears commonly in ancient Judah and Israel.9 They contain references to the deity, often to affirm a child as a fulfillment of a promise or to express gratitude to God for the birth of a child. In Hebrew, theophoric names contain the Hebrew yah (an abbreviation for Yahweh), el (one of the Hebrew words for God), or baal (meaning “Lord”). The name Micah (mîkāh) ends with yāh suffix in Hebrew, as is perhaps more evident in the fuller spelling of the name in Jer 26:18 (mîkāyāh). The name consists of the interrogative particle mî (“Who?”), the preposition k (“like”) and the abbreviation yāh (“Yahweh”). The name means “Who is like Yahweh?” The name functions as a declaration of faith and gratitude. The name implies gratitude that Yahweh has delivered on the promise of an heir.

Moresheth was likely a village about twenty miles southwest of Jerusalem in the Shephelah, though its precise location has been a matter of long-standing debate.10 Portions of the Shephelah represented contested land because the boundaries separating Judah from Philistine territory changed periodically. In Mic 1:14, the same village is called Moresheth-Gath, which is one of the towns threatened by Assyrian advances at the end of the eighth century BCE. Gath was also one of the five major cities of Philistia. Identifying Moresheth as the hometown of Micah has long been interpreted to mean that the prophet was not part of the Jerusalemite inner circle of religious leaders.11 In some ways, one can envision Micah the prophet somewhat like Amos and Jeremiah, meaning they were not part of the Jerusalem power structure related to the temple or the king. Amos came from a Judean village called Tekoa a few miles south of Jerusalem, but most of his speeches target the Northern Kingdom, particularly the societal elite in Samaria (Amos 3:9, 12; 4:1; 6:1; 8:14) and its religious leaders in Bethel (Amos 3:14; 4:4; 5:5–6; 7:10–17). The book portrays Amos as challenging Israel’s leaders, even though the officials of Bethel and Samaria rejected Amos and expelled him back to Judah (Amos 7:10–17). Jeremiah came from a small village just north of Jerusalem called Anathoth, and he spoke vehemently against the kings, priests, and people in Jerusalem. Yet, Jeremiah had powerful connections to the corridors of power in Jerusalem, especially through the family of Baruch the scribe.12 Micah’s Moreshite background likely made him an outsider in Jerusalem’s political circles (to some degree), but that does not mean that Micah had no allies. His words are recalled at the trial of Jeremiah roughly a century after Micah purportedly pronounced judgment against Jerusalem to Hezekiah (see the discussion of Mic 3:12 for details).

Micah 1:1 mentions three Judean kings: Jotham (756–741 BCE), Ahaz (741–725 BCE), and Hezekiah (725–696 BCE). Together, this trio creates difficulties for those interpreting Micah as an independent prophetic writing. The reigns of these three kings cover more than sixty years, and for Micah to have served during the reigns of all three kings, he would need to have served as a prophet for at least sixteen years (741–725 BCE). Scholars raise at least two problems regarding these three successive Judean kings. First, most of the material that scholars assign to the eighth-century prophet appears only in the first three chapters of the book, which means that the prophetic material that might have direct ties to Micah would only represent a small selection of oracles and speeches the prophet would have delivered over such a lengthy career.13 Second, by most reckonings, the eighth-century material contained in Mic 1–3 relates to events in the time of Hezekiah’s reign. None of it can be reliably dated to the reigns of Jotham or Ahaz.14 The naming of Jotham and Ahaz need not be inaccurate, but the book contains no material from the time of the earlier kings. Two possibilities could explain the reference to Jotham and Ahaz. One solution is to assume that the person who added the superscription knew other traditions about Micah that placed him in these earlier time periods. In this scenario, the writer simply alluded to those traditions by including all three kings. A second solution, and the one preferred in this commentary, is that the mention of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah was created or enhanced by editors in the exilic period as a means of creating a chronological framework when Micah was attached to the same scroll as Hosea and Amos (or Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah).15 Hosea 1:1 lists five kings: Uzziah (791–739 BCE), Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, all kings of Judah, and Jeroboam II (786–746 BCE), king of Israel. The first and last of these kings were essentially coterminous with one another as kings of Judah and Israel respectively, but the author did not list the kings of Israel who reigned during the time of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (kings of Judah). Uzziah and Jeroboam (the first and last king mentioned in Hos 1:1) essentially cover the first half of the eighth century BCE while Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah cover the second half. Zephaniah 1:1 completes this chronological system by tracing Zephaniah’s genealogy from Josiah (640–609 BCE) backward to the prophet’s great-great-grandfather Hezekiah. Likely, the three kings mentioned in Mic 1:1 were added in the exilic period when the four writings (Hosea, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah) were joined to one another.16 Apart from the role of creating a chronological frame that becomes the backbone of the chronological arrangement of the Book of the Twelve (along with Haggai and Zechariah), the reference to the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah provides the reader with directions for understanding the setting for Micah. While critical scholarship has dated much of Mic 4–7 to the exilic period and beyond, little doubt exists that these later additions were intended to be read as though they come from the eighth-century prophet.17

The concluding clause of 1:1 describes the content of Micah as the word which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. This final clause stands out in several ways. First, the antecedent to the relative pronoun which refers all the way back to the first word of the verse (dābār). The ʾăšer clause reads like an afterthought because ʾăšer is so far removed from the word it modifies. Second, a large percentage of Micah (1–3 and 4–7) concerns the fate of Jerusalem, but references to Samaria appear only in 1:5–7. This last clause in 1:1 thus anticipates the material in 1:5–7. Yet, careful analysis of 1:5–7 indicates that these verses were added during the exilic updating of Micah that connected early traditions of Micah with Hosea and Amos (see discussion of 1:5–7). Like the mention of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, the mention of Samaria in 1:1 refers to traditions in Micah that presuppose Jerusalem’s destruction. These verses warn Jerusalem to cease imitating the idolatry of the Northern Kingdom but presume Samaria’s destruction.

It seems plausible that the four parts of the superscription were not all created simultaneously. The reference to the three Judean kings and the inclusion of Samaria reflect the updates to Micah that are best dated to the exilic period.18 This redaction was concerned, in part, with creating redactional links to exilic versions of Hosea and Amos, and (probably later) to Zephaniah (see esp. the discussion of Mic 4:6–7, which is cited by Zeph 3:19–20). Regarding the earliest form of Mic 1:1 prior to the addition of the kings and the reference to Samaria, one may logically and plausibly assume that the prophet’s identity was included along with the hometown, especially since it appears in 1:14.19





B. YAHWEH COMES FOR JUDGMENT (1:2–7)


2Listen, all youa peoples. Draw near, earth and itsb fullness for the Lord Yahweh will bec a witness againstd you; the Lord from his holy temple.

3For behold,e Yahweh going forth from his place. He will come downf and tread upon the high places of the earth.

4The mountains melt beneath him, and the valleys burst open like wax before fire, like water poured down a slope.

5All of this is for the rebellion of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the sin of Jacob? Is it not Samaria?g And what are the high places of Judah?h Is it not Jerusalem?

6And I willi make Samaria into a heap of rubblej in the field, to a planting place for a vineyard, and I will hurl her stones into the valley. And I will uncover her foundations.

7And all her idols will be smashed, and all her earnings will be burned in the fire. And all her idols I will make a desolation, for she collected themk from a prostitute’s earnings so they will return to a prostitute’s earnings.

a. The MT has “all of them” (kullām), which is at odds with 1:2a, which addresses the nations with a second-person masculine plural imperative. The changing of person from second person to third person is common in vocative constructions. See GKC §144p. The second half of this expression also uses a second-person verb and a third-person suffix on the noun. See text note b. The translation you merely reflects the same idea as the MT using an idiomatic English expression.

b. The MT addresses the earth and refers to its fullness using a third-person feminine singular suffix on the noun məlōʾāh. The changing of person from second person to third person is common in vocative constructions. See GKC §144p. See text note a.

c. In English, the LXX means “and the Lord will be.” The LXX modifies this phrase from the Hebrew in two ways. First, the LXX reflects a different MT pointing of the verb “to be.” The Greek verb is a future indicative (estai), which is typically used to translate the vav-consecutive form in Hebrew (wayəhî). The Masoretes, however, pointed the Hebrew verb as a jussive (wîhî), which means “let the Lord be.” These two verbs reflect the same consonantal text in Hebrew (wyhw), so the unpointed source text of the Greek was not different. The LXX also simplifies the Lord Yahweh to “Lord” (kurios), but this regularly happens elsewhere in the LXX when Yahweh is combined with ʾadōnai. See, for example, Isa 10:23, 24; 22:12, 15; 25:8; 28:16; Jer 1:6; 2:22; 4:10; 7:20; Ezek 2:4; 3:11; Amos 1:8; 4:2; 6:8; 7:1, 4, 5. The divergences in the Greek thus reflect accommodations to the Greek target audience. The use of for here could accommodate either pointing since the vav-consecutive can imply causality (because) and the jussive conveys volition (that he might). Relatedly, in one Hebrew manuscript, 1Q 14, and one Greek manuscript, 8Ḥev 1, the divine name is written in an archaic Hebrew script (see the discussion of this phenomenon in “The Text of Micah”). The result is visually stunning, particularly in 8Ḥev 1 since one does not expect to see Hebrew in a Greek text.

d. 1Q14 has a different word order for the phrase “Lord Yahweh will be.” Whereas the MT follows the normal syntax of putting the verb first, 1Q14 lists Yahweh Adonai first, perhaps for emphasis. The meaning does not change at all, but it is difficult to determine which is the earlier reading.

e. BHS Suggests hinnēhû (“behold, he”) rather than hinnēh yhwh (“behold, Yahweh”) on the basis of meter. Meter, however, should not override early manuscript evidence, which attests the Tetragrammaton, in both Greek (LXX, 8Ḥev 1) and Hebrew (1Q14; Mur 88; MT).

f. BHS suggests that both yrd (descend) and drk (tread) are unnecessary. Quite a number of Greek manuscripts omit the first verb, though both Rahlfs and the Göttingen edition of the LXX include both verbs in the base text.20 Further, Mur 88 in Hebrew and 8Ḥev 1 in Greek show two verbs are present (though some of the letters are missing or damaged). 1Q14 has a lacuna at this point. MT is preferred.

g. One Greek witness (8Ḥev 1) reads Samaroia rather than Samariea, though it might simply be a variant spelling in the Greek. The name Samaria appears in two other places in Micah (1:1, 6), but while neither of those is extant in 8Ḥev 1, the editors reconstruct the text using the otherwise unattested spelling Samaroia. Unfortunately, none of the other texts in the Book of the Twelve that mention Samaria (Hos 7:1; 8:5–6; 10:5; 13:16; Amos 3:9, 12; 4:1; 6:1; 8:14; Obad 19; Mic 1:1, 5–6) are extant in 8Ḥev 1. On the other hand, it seems unwise to reconstruct the form in 1:1, 6 based on this one instance, unattested anywhere else.

h. The LXX has the phrase “the house of Judah” rather than merely Judah. All the manuscripts in Hebrew (1Q14, Mur 88) and Greek (8Ḥev 1) from the Judean Desert agree with MT, meaning that MT is preferred. The Old Greek translator probably made this change to form a better parallel to “house of Israel” earlier in the verse.

i. MT points this verb in a way that indicates the Masoretes understood the destruction to point toward the future. In the unpointed Hebrew text, the same verb could be interpreted as the consequences of the previous action. In other words, while my translation reflects the MT pointing, shifting the accent from the final syllable to the penultimate syllable would mean that the verb form in unpointed Hebrew could be pronounced as an inverted perfect to show continuity with the previous action (see Joüon, §119). In any event, the future action concerns the action of the theophany, and does not necessarily help in dating the text.

j. The text notes in critical editions of MT (BHK3, BHS, and BHQ) reflect changes in how scholars deal with unusual forms. All three editions include the Masoretic notes in the margin of the Leningrad Codex, which labels this word as a hapax legomenon. BHK3 notes that the LXX renders the word ʿî (meaning pile of rubble) as hopōrophuakion, which translates as “hut” (the kind used by workers in the field for protection). This Greek word appears only five times (Isa 1:8; 24:20; Mic 1:6; 3:12; Ps 78:1), usually in plural. As a result, BHK assumes that ʿî was not original and suggests either replacing heap with yaʿar (meaning “forest”), pointing to Ezek 20:46 (21:2) or simply to omit the Hebrew word heap (ʿî) altogether (while keeping the preposition). The resulting translation of the former would be “I will make Samaria into a forest of the field,” and could assume that the vine (mentioned at the end of Mic 1:6) would grow over the city of Samaria. The translation of the latter would be I will make Samaria “into […] a field.” BHS by contrast notes the LXX wording, but makes no suggestion to replace the MT as the original text, leaving open the question of which reading is original by showing no preference. BHQ simply notes that the word is a hapax legomenon by recording the marginal notes of the Leningrad codex, but does not have any kind of text-critical note or discussion of heap (ʿî) in the text, thus ignoring the variant in the Greek text completely. BHQ thus assumes the LXX represents a paraphrastic translation that cannot be used to determine the original text of Mic 1:6. Looking at these three critical editions demonstrates a dramatic shift in how scholars deal with variant readings in the LXX. They have become much less confident that such variations automatically point to a different text even though the Old Greek text of the LXX predates the earliest manuscripts from Qumran and the Judean Desert. The LXX must be first evaluated as a translation and a text that has its own literary form. Often, it is closely related to the MT (esp. in the unpointed text), but the translator of the Twelve had to produce a text that made sense to the Greek audience even while trying to reflect the Hebrew source text it was translating.

k. Them is assumed to complete the thought. The expectation of an accusative with this verb collected and the next line completes the thought but also assumes the identity of the idols with a plural verb.

The unit begins with a call to attention to all the peoples of the world (1:2), followed by a theophany report (1:3–4), and a warning to Jerusalem and Judah concerning impending judgment (1:5–7). The call to attention has been interpreted in numerous ways based upon how one understands the reference to the nations and the role of the witness. Scholars have interpreted the nations as: (1) the object of judgment within a theophany report; (2) the witnesses to a warrior-king’s departure from his palace that is associated with the theophany; (3) witnesses in the trial scene that follows; (4) a rhetorical device in an oral performance of a prophetic preacher; or (5) the object of judgment that foreshadows chapters 4–5 that were appended to the book in the Persian period.

Some confusion exists concerning the role of the nations and Yahweh’s role as witness depending upon how commentators construct the action and the relationship of 1:2b to the surrounding context. Most interpret the nations as the object of judgment for the theophany description that follows in 1:3–4, 3–7, or 1:3–9.21 Nevertheless, some contest this reading. Terence Fretheim follows the LXX understanding of 1:2bα that Yahweh will appear “among you” rather than against you. He is unusual in treating the nations as part of Yahweh’s army who will accompany Yahweh as he goes forth to battle Judah. Helmut Utzschneider is atypical in arguing that the pronouncement of vengeance on the nations is the first act of the book of Micah, but that it has no inherent connection to 1:3–4. More commonly, scholars argue 1:2 introduces 1:3–4 (which Utzschneider calls the second appearance of Yahweh). Artur Weiser sees the theophany as a later insertion that mistakenly associates the prophet of the book of Micah with Micah ben Imlah in 1 Kgs 22:28. For Weiser, the theophany introduces a single event in which the entire world is called to suffer when God appears, but this idea has no parallel elsewhere in Micah or the Nebi’im. Weiser is typical of older commentators who erroneously import the concept of universal judgment into Micah based on a few New Testament texts regarding expectations of the end of days as taught by systematic theologians.

For some, the nations are treated as witnesses to the departure of Yahweh as warrior in 1:2 that is typical of theophany reports.22 For many in this group, Yahweh appears as a warrior going forth to battle his enemies.

Others interpret the prophet’s statement that Yahweh will be a witness against you in 1:2bα as the prophet describing Yahweh’s role in a juridical process.23 For them, the nations are not the object of judgment in 1:3–7 but are called upon to witness the action of Yahweh in punishing Judah and Jerusalem. Recently, however, a number of scholars have argued convincingly that this role of the witness of the nations has no analogues elsewhere in the Old Testament.24 Parallels cited by the first group appear in Deut 32:1 and Isa 1:2, but the authors of the second group argue that the witnesses in those cases are cosmic entities (heavens and earth) and hence would be different than the human entities (peoples and earth) cited in Mic 1:2. The cosmic entities could be present with Yahweh in ways that humans could not.

The portrait of the theophany in 1:3–4 also gives rise to debate about its integrity within 1:2–7 and the book of Micah, since this theophanic element is unique in Micah.25 Several scholars have argued, consequently, that 1:3–4 was inserted. Aaron Schart emphasizes the unique form in Micah, and sees it in relationship to editing of the Book of the Four (Hosea, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah).26 Jakob Wöhrle sees 1:3–4 as part of the Grundlage since 1:5a references “all this” and 1:3–4 represents the only possible unit to which “this” could refer.27 Wöhrle’s observation correctly identifies a problem with Schart’s proposal that 1:3–4 was added after 1:5, 6–7.

Micah 1:3–4 describes Yahweh’s appearance in poetic form, and in prophetic literature theophanies presuppose judgment. Nevertheless, while Yahweh’s appearance affects the mountains and the valleys, 1:3–4 do not specify the object of Yahweh’s wrath. Some scholars have therefore read 1:3–4 with 1:2 or 2a. The descriptions of the effects upon the mountains and valleys evoke the immensity of Yahweh’s presence, not the object of wrath. For this reason as well, Wöhrle is correct that 1:5 presupposes 1:3–4. The theophany assumes not merely that “all of this” is happening because of sin, but also the identity of the entity being judged, with 1:5 rendering these assumptions explicit through the pronouncement against Jacob, Israel, Judah, and Samaria.

Micah 1:5–7 threaten Judah and Jerusalem with the same type of judgment experienced by Samaria (and the Northern Kingdom). As such, the verses presuppose Samaria’s destruction (722 BCE), but seem to treat that event as something in the recent past. Yet, scholars generally interpret 1:8–16 in light of Sennacherib’s campaign (701 BCE) some twenty years after Samaria’s destruction.





1. Theophany Report against the Nations (1:2)


2 Rhetorically, this verse functions as a call to attention and the beginning of an indictment. As such it functions well as part of the theophany report that follows in 1:3–4. Nevertheless, the indictment in 1:2b assumes that Yahweh will come to judge the nations while 1:5–7 assume that Samaria has been judged and Jerusalem is about to be judged. It is thus not clear how 1:2b relates to the action in 1:3–7. Hans Walter Wolff notes several examples where a summons to all nations is followed by calls to witness judgment against a specific nation.28 Wolff’s examples demonstrate that thematically and form-critically, it is possible to invoke the nations to witness the judgment of another nation. Grammatically, however, the language used in the key phrase in Mic 1:2bα relates to the question of whether the presence of witness in connection to a b preposition means “witness against you” or “witness among you” in Mic 1:2. The idiom ʿēd … b lines up best with the former, which means one should translate the phrase as “witness against you” since no other Old Testament text uses the phrase to mean “among.”29 That being said, at least three explanations for the origin of the verse also affect how various commentators talk about this verse.30 The verse (or a portion of it) may be treated as (1) an isolated saying of the prophet;31 (2) a redactional gloss connecting to a broader context (inside and/or outside Micah);32 or (3) an essential part of the prophet Micah’s speech.33

Micah 1:2a consists of two parallel lines wherein two commands delivered to a group are followed by a vocative identifying the group being addressed (Listen, all you peoples. Draw near, earth and its fullness). The vocatives (all you peoples, the earth and its fullness) address foreign nations. The parallel verbs (listen, draw near) command the groups to pay attention. Each verb addresses the subject. The masculine plural imperative listen addresses the masculine plural noun peoples, while draw near uses a feminine singular imperative since earth is feminine singular. It ignores the second portion of the vocative (and all its fullness).34 The call to attention in 1:2a functions meaningfully as an introduction to the theophany report in 1:3–7 where Judah and Jerusalem are the intended target of Yahweh’s appearance while 1:2bα (And the Lord Yahweh will be a witness against you) presupposes a juridical scene and presupposes the nations as the object of the theophany. In reading the verse in the tradition of a theophany, the jussive sense of the MT does not fit well, but the LXX indicates that some read the consonants as a vav-consecutive. Two recent commentaries avoid the jussive sense altogether, meaning they implicitly follow the pointing presumed by the LXX pronunciation.35 Commentators do not understand the juridical terminology in the same way. Some assume that the nations are witnesses to the trial scene and treat 1:2a as an invitation to the nations to serve as a witness (either a witness to the entire trial proceedings or as a witness for the prosecuting attorney, Yahweh, against Israel). Since 1:5–7 unambiguously describes judgment against Israel and threatens Judah and Jerusalem, these commentators interpret the nations as witnesses for the prosecution. Some assume the nations will witness Yahweh’s judgment against Israel.36 Others interpret 1:2 as an invitation to take the witness seat to testify to the veracity of what Yahweh will say as the prosecutor.37 Interpreting the nations as a witness at the trial has become more difficult to support since the work of J. T. Willis, who demonstrates that the Hebrew idiom in 1:2 only appears elsewhere in contexts where a witness accuses someone of something untoward.38 Thus, in 1:2aβ, the narrator presupposes Yahweh is the witness accusing the nations of a crime.

Consequently, Mic 1:2 as a whole appears to present two different messages regarding the role of the peoples: as a witness to Yahweh’s ensuing judgment in 1:2a and as the object of Yahweh’s judgment in 1:2bα. The final line (1:2bβ) fits either scenario (the Lord from his holy temple). A theophany refers to the appearance of God. In prophetic literature, the description of a theophany generally narrates God’s future appearance to pronounce judgment, and the theophanic report follows an established pattern.39 The theophany (without 1:2bα) has a clear structure: a call to attention (1:2a), a description proper of Yahweh’s appearance (1:3–4), and the implications (1:5–7). The object of the theophany (without 1:2bα) is Yahweh’s own people in 1:3–7, but when the gloss is added in 1:2bα (And the Lord Yahweh will be a witness against you), the location makes the nations the only possible antecedent. As many have noted, the juridical scene and the punishment of the nations fit better with later redactional strands of Mic 4–5, but only one phrase (1:2bα) makes that association. The final portion (1:2bβ): The Lord from his holy temple) could belong to the original pronouncement as it merely states that the Lord (ʾădōnāy) is located at the heavenly temple, a location that is assumed in the opening portion of 1:3 (for behold Yahweh going forth from his place). Hence, 1:2bβ announces the Lord is coming from his holy palace in the heavens and 1:3 begins with a statement that Yahweh is going forth from his place.

The Hebrew word translated as temple is hêkāl, and it refers to a large house (or palace when the house belongs to the king). When referring to the house of Yahweh, the word hêkāl can refer to Yahweh’s heavenly dwelling (e.g., Isa 6:1) or to the earthly temple (e.g., Jer 7:2; Hag 2:15) that represents Yahweh’s home in Jerusalem. It is not always easy to distinguish one from the other in every text. The connections from 1:2a and 1:2bβ make sense without 1:2bα, and connect well to that which follows. The insertion of 1:2bα not only changes the object of judgment (presumably anticipating Mic 4–5), it also makes sense that it uses both terms for God used in parallel in the surrounding context, Adonai (in 1:2bβ) and Yahweh (in 1:3). The original form of the verse that introduces the theophany, then, looked as follows:

2aListen, all you peoples.

Draw near, O earth and its fullness.

2bβThe Lord (is coming) from his holy temple.

3For behold, Yahweh is about to go forth from his place.

2bαAnd the Lord (ʾădōnāy) Yahweh will be a witness against you;



Thus, Mic 1:2 makes good sense as the call to attention for the theophany (1:3–7), but the object of the theophany in 1:2bα is not the same as the object of the theophany in 1:3–7. The insertion of the juridical statement in 1:2bα assumes the nations are the object of punishment, not merely the witnesses to Yahweh’s actions against Jerusalem and Judah. This insertion is not an isolated gloss, but a redactional gloss that anticipates the themes of later portions of the book.





2. Theophany Description (1:3–4)


3 Micah 1:3 and 1:4 function as a theophany report and are almost universally recognized as inherently unified. As such, the verses narrate Yahweh’s action as a warrior who leaves the divine palace to execute judgment on someone or something.40 Micah 1:3 is unusual, however, because it states explicitly that Yahweh’s palace resides in the heavens rather than on a mountain or in the temple. The action described in Mic 1:3–4 should be noted, as it has an effect upon how one understands 1:2 as well as the relationship of 1:3–4 to 1:5. First, the point of origin of Yahweh’s movement is Yahweh’s heavenly abode in 1:3. Something rouses Yahweh from his place in 1:3. The statement coincides with the last statement in 1:2 that portrays Yahweh as in his holy temple. The image of Yahweh going forth from his temple to the earth implies judgment. Second, debate exists concerning whether high places in this context denotes the same idea of high place as in 1:5. Micah 1:5 portrays the high place(s) in a polemical fashion, similar to those places of illicit worship castigated in the Deuteronomistic History.41 By contrast, most scholars interpret high places in 1:3 as mountains on the basis of 1:4 and the language of theophanies in general.42 The parallelism in 1:3–4 suggests as much and warns against associating the polemical tone of high places in Kings with the high places in Mic 1:3. The mountains (high places) in 1:3 are not the target of Yahweh’s judgment, they merely suffer as a result of Yahweh’s presence because they cannot bear his weight.

4 Micah 1:4 continues the theophany from 1:3 by narrating the consequences of Yahweh’s march through the land. The immensity of Yahweh’s presence takes a dramatic toll on the earth. As Yahweh treads upon the high places, they are unable to bear the weight of his presence. Consequently, the mountains are said to melt beneath him and the valleys split open. The imagery depicts the land’s inability to hold Yahweh, especially Yahweh’s anger. The inability of the earth to hold Yahweh is noted elsewhere in the poetic imagery of prophetic texts. For example, in Isa 66:1 Yahweh claims the entire earth is Yahweh’s footstool so that a temple becomes far too small to hold Yahweh. This claim challenges the tradition that the temple itself is Yahweh’s footstool (1 Chr 28:2; Ps 132:7; see also Zion in Lam 2:1; Ps 99:5). Micah 1:4 shares the presupposition with some of these later texts that Yahweh dwells in the heavens, and such articulations do become more common in the Persian and Hellenistic eras. Nevertheless, even theophanies that speak of specific mountains as the home of deities often do not represent literal statements in this respect. Mountaintops appear as the entry point for deities to come and go between the heavens and the earth. They represent the place where a deity dwelled, which likely conceptualized a world beyond the earth where the lives of the gods unfolded, though they also intersect with human reality.43 In other words, the divine palace was considered to be so far up the mountain that one could not see it from the ground, and in this sense it resided in the heavens.





3. Threat against Judah after Samaria’s Destruction (1:5–7)


5 Only with 1:5 does the object of Yahweh’s wrath become clear. As it currently stands, the verse offers a complex set of parallel statements and questions as a means of indicting both Samaria and Jerusalem for the judgment depicted in the theophany (1:3–4). Yet, the compositional integrity of this verse has been questioned, as has its relationship to the larger unit.44 These arguments notwithstanding, stronger and less arbitrary arguments exist for including the bulk of 1:3–7 as a coherent, unified introduction to a collection of Micah speeches that were published in the exilic period, a corpus that extended to at least 3:12.45 Jeremias separates only 1:5b as a later addition to 1:3–7, but even 1:5b can be read as a meaningful part of 1:2–7 if one considers the larger literary horizon in relationship to 3:12. Jeremias correctly notes, as have others, that 1:5a serves as a necessary bridge between the theophany (1:3–4) and the judgment pronounced in 1:6–7 while 1:5b assumes that Jacob means the Northern Kingdom, that is, Israel. Jeremias astutely notes that this assumption runs counter to the times the phrase Jacob (or house of Jacob) is used in foundational material in Micah (3:1, 8–9; cf. 1:14–15; 2:7). All the other references to Jacob in Micah assume that Jacob refers to Judah. The association of the guilt of Samaria and Jerusalem in 1:5a connects meaningfully to 1:1, 7 and 3:12.

1:5a This (punishment) assumes the theophany in 1:3–4 will happen because of the rebellion of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel.

1:5b links logically to the reference to Samaria in 1:1b and creates a north/south parallel by referring to Yahweh’s decision to punish both Samaria and Jerusalem together. It connects the high places of Judah with Jerusalem, assuming that Jerusalem represents the high point of Judah. The verse also assumes Samaria is evidence of the sins of Jacob. Finally, it takes up the vocabulary of the high places from 1:3 (which referred to the mountains as the high places of the earth, thereby assuming they reach into the heavens).

1:6 describes the destruction of Jerusalem using an analogy of a farmer tilling a field whereby Jerusalem is left like a bump (high place) in the field where the blade has plowed it, while the devastation has lasted so long that trees have grown around the bump.

1:7 describes the destruction of idols using the word pāsîl, which probably refers to carved images. The verse links logically with 1:5a because the mere existence of such idols would imply rebellion against Yahweh’s covenant command. The use of such idols would constitute sin.

3:12 Yahweh pronounces that Jerusalem will be destroyed because of the people being confronted by the prophet. The agricultural imagery in 3:12 implies Yahweh will destroy Jerusalem like a farmer tills the soil. Yahweh will overturn Jerusalem so that the place where it once stood looks like a freshly plowed field, and it will be deserted so long that trees will have grown in its place while the temple mountain that used to tower will look like a bump in a forest because Jerusalem will no longer physically exist.

In a real sense, then, 1:5a appears to be part of a text composed to introduce Mic 1–3. It is not part of a fragmented speech. The word this (zôʾt) assumes an impending punishment whose most logical antecedent would be the punishment implied in the events described in 1:3–4 (the theophany). Further it contains one of three references to high places (see also 1:4, 5; and 3:12) where each successive reference to the high places (bāmōt) appears smaller. In the theophany (1:3–4), Yahweh tramples across the highest mountains of the earth that reach into the heavens. At the appearance of Yahweh, those mountainous high places [bāmōt] melt like wax before a fire. In 1:5a, the prophetic speaker asks a rhetorical question: What are all the high places [bāmōt] of Judah? The prophet then follows immediately with a second question that answers the first: Is it not Jerusalem? Here, however, Jerusalem is referenced with a feminine singular pronoun (this). In essence, the prophetic speaker claims Jerusalem is the tallest mountain of Judah (though literally it is not). In 1:5, however, the city of Jerusalem is named the high place of Judah, but the verse uses the plural form of bāmâ (bāmōt) to refer to Jerusalem. In 1:6, the farmer tills Jerusalem like a field and the high place turns into nothing more than a bump in the dirt (bāmōt), metaphorically speaking, a small berm in the field.

At this point, however, it should also be noted that Mic 1:5b creates the connective logic that helps transition to 1:6–7 (which in turn links to 1:8–16) and to 3:12. The fact that 1:5b equates the sin of the north with the sin of Judah is precisely the point of 1:1b. Together, 1:5a and 1:5b effectively equate the transgression of Jacob and the house of Israel with the sin of Samaria and the high places of Judah. The threat is clear: if Samaria has been punished, then Jerusalem should take note since her fate will be the same if nothing changes.46 The two parts of 1:5 then work in tandem to introduce the dual themes of 1:6–7 (destruction of Samaria) and 1:8–16 (the imminent threat to Jerusalem), especially as indicated in the editorial insertions of 1:9b and 1:12b.

6 Micah 1:6 flows seamlessly into 1:7, interprets the significance of 1:5b, and anticipates the climactic pronouncement of Mic 3:12. In so doing, both verses refer to Samaria’s destruction while subtly connecting its destruction with the impending destruction of Jerusalem. Recent scholarship has treated 1:6–7 as a text from the exilic or postexilic period. Theodor Lescow labels 1:6–7 an insertion dated in the middle of the fourth century BCE.47 Schart, Wöhrle, and Jeremias also consider these verses later interpretations, but from the exilic period.48 For Schart, the verses form part of the compositional layer of the introduction to Mic 1–3 (1:2b, 5a, 6–8) created in the exilic period because they evince Hosea and Amos before the addition of two more insertions.49 Wöhrle does not consider 1:6–7 as part of his foundational layer of the introduction (1:1, 3–5a, 8), but includes the verses (along with 1:5b; i.e., 1:5b–7) with his Deuteronomistic layer (1:5b–7; 5:9–13; 6:2–4a, 9–15), which he places in the late exilic period.50 Wöhrle argues that 1:6–7 represents a later addition because its language and its subject do not come into play elsewhere in Micah; this rationale is not strong enough to overcome the fact that without 1:6–7, the theophany of 1:3–4 does not have a clear target or rationale.51

The language used in these verses does triple duty. First, the language of these verses picks up the language of the theophany in 1:3–4. Second, the language continues the idea of 1:5 that Samaria is the primary target of Yahweh’s wrath that was announced in 1:3–4. Third, these verses anticipate Mic 3:12. On this last point, Schart correctly notes the presence of allusions to the language of Hosea and Amos in 1:6–7.52 The Hosea allusions in 1:6 imply the idea that Samaria’s destruction should serve as a warning to Jerusalem, an assumption that 1:6 makes explicit. This connection evokes parallels to Hosea that presuppose the finding of the Torah in the time of Josiah long after the death of the prophet Micah.

Micah 1:6 pronounces judgment upon Samaria and anticipates the message of Mic 3:12, which pronounces the same judgment will befall Jerusalem. Recent scholarship points out that 1:6 indicates Samaria will become a heap (of rubble) in the field which reflects virtually the same language used of Jerusalem in 3:12.53 Micah 1:6 means that Mic 1–3 depicts the two judgments in parallel terms; 1:6 displays a close affinity to 1:5, and its cumbersome association of high places with Samaria and Jerusalem. Since 1:6 appears as part of the introductory unit of the book, and 3:12 represents the last verse of Mic 1–3 (an important block in the structure of the book), one may surmise that someone conceptualized this composition of Mic 1–3 from the beginning. It does not, therefore, suggest that someone was writing down short sayings. As such, 1:6 helps to create an inclusio between the first and last units of Mic 1–3, which in turn suggests that chapters 1–3 existed in written form before chapters 4–7 were incorporated into the book of Micah. This inclusion, in all probability, was not created prior to the reforms of Josiah in 622, or at seventy to eighty years after the prophet Micah died. It might even have been created after the production of the exilic version of Kings in 560 BCE (which would have been 160 years after the siege of Sennacherib). Micah 1:3–7 uses Jacob to mean the Northern Kingdom while the rest of chapters 1–3 use the name Jacob to refer to Judah. Micah 1:3–7 thus introduces a form of the book of Micah that was compiled from smaller sources well after the time of the prophet, but the content of the individual units within 1:2–3:12 focuses very clearly upon interpreting events from the prophet’s lifetime in the eighth century.

7 Most of the key words in Mic 1:7 have parallels in Hosea. These key terms include idols (cf. Hos 4:17; 8:4; 11:2; 13:2), prostitute (cf. Hos 1:2; 2:7; 3:3; 4:10, 12–15, 18; 5:3; 9:1), and earnings (cf. Hos 9:1). These lexical parallels have been connected with the language of Hosea since as early as the work of Alfred Jepsen.54 Although some commentators treat the similar language as a sign of direct dependence of one eighth-century prophet upon another, recent scholars have understood the allusions as the work of a later writer who presupposes the finding of the book of the law in 622 BCE or from the time of the exile (probably one working on the Book of the Four).55

In any event, these recent scholarly investigations make sense of Mic 1:6–7 as part of a redactional text that is keenly aware of its immediate and extended context. The passage seeks to interpret the prophet’s role in communicating Yahweh’s desires to Yahweh’s people throughout the major events of the last quarter of the eighth century. Micah 1–3 presents a prophet who challenges Judah and Jerusalem to learn from Samaria’s destruction and stop worshiping idols and learn to practice justice instead, thereby extending the message of Hosea and Amos, who challenged the leaders of the Northern Kingdom to do the same. Micah 1:6–7 challenges Judah’s worship of idols much as Hosea did. Micah 2 (esp.) challenges the ethical shortcomings of the Southern Kingdom, much as Amos did for the Northern Kingdom. Amos also presented Yahweh’s message to the surrounding nations (1:3–2:3) before turning to threaten Judah and Israel (Amos 2:4–5; 2:6–16). In the next unit (Mic 1:8–16), the prophet addresses the reactions of the foreign entities as Assyria threatens the Phoenicians, the Philistines, and Judah prior to the siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE. Micah 1–3 thus confronts both the Northern and the Southern Kingdoms for their ethical and theological shortcomings that break the covenant stipulations regarding the worship of Yahweh and the treatment of other human beings.





C. THE PROPHET LAMENTS AND CALLS THE SHEPHELAH TO DO THE SAME (1:8–16)


8Because of this I will lament and wail. I will walk naked and barefoot. I will make lamentation like the jackals and mourning like the daughters of the ostrich.

9Indeed, her wound is incurable for it has come to Judah, reaching to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem.

10Do not declare it in Gath; do not weep in Beth–Leaphrah.a Rollb around in the dust.

11Pass by for yourselves, the inhabitant of Shaphir; the nakedness and shame. The inhabitant of Zenaan does not go forth. The wailing of the house of Azel will take its support from you.

12For the inhabitant of Maroth writhes for good because calamity from Yahweh has descended to the gate of Jerusalem.

13Attach the chariot to the steeds, inhabitant of Lachish. She was the beginning of sin for Lady Zion, for the rebellions of Israel were found in you.

14Therefore, give Moresheth-Gathc a parting gift.d The houses of Achzibe will be a deception for the kings of Israel.

15Again, I will bring to you the one who takes possession, inhabitant of Mareshah. The glory of Israel will go to Adullam.

16Cut your hair; shave because of the children of your luxury. Enlarge your bald spot like the eagle for they have been exiled from you.

a. Literally, the House of Dust.

b. The ketîb in the MT means, “I will roll around,” thus correcting the change of speaker’s first-person speech with third -person feminine singular speech. The qērê reading is a feminine singular imperative, “Roll around!” The feminine singular assumes the city as the addressee, which is typically feminine in Hebrew. The LXX has a plural imperative, but that merely adapts to the Greek practice of referring to collectives with plural verbs. It does not indicate a different text. The previous verbs (declare, weep) in 1:10 are masculine plural so the LXX—as elsewhere—simplifies the changing verb forms into a consistent one (see Amos 9:11, e.g., where three different pronouns in the MT become one in the LXX). While it is difficult to decide the question of the original reading, the feminine singular imperative is probably original, while the first-person form represents an adaptation—perhaps to strengthen the pun on the verb so as to draw attention to the Philistines.

c. The LXX does not name Moresheth-Gath as the town, but merely has Gath (get). Instead, the LXX translates the unpointed Hebrew conanants (šlwḥym) with “inheritance” (klēronomias, a Greek word that often translates some form of yrš). The Greek translator thus translates as “an inheritance of Gath” instead of Moresheth Gath. See the next note on “parting gift” for the full translation.

d. The LXX translates parting gift (šlwḥym) as a plural participle from šlḥ (meaning “send forth”). Combined with the previous phrase, this line in the LXX attempts to make sense of the Hebrew consonants, but the result is even more muddled than the Hebrew text because of the number of dependent clauses involved in the Greek. The full translation on Mic 1:14 reads as follows: “Therefore, you shall give worthless houses—ones being dispatched—as far as the inheritance of Geth. It became meaningless to the kings of Israel” (NETS).

e. The LXX apparently emphasizes the Hebrew pun in 1:14 by creating a word play in Greek.56 The Hebrew word for deception (ʾākzāb) and the town name Achzib (ʾākzîb) both come from the same triliteral root (kzb) that means “to lie” or “deceive.” The LXX eliminates the “town” name from the phrase houses of Achzib (bātêʾākzîb) and translates that phrase as “vain houses” (oikous mataious) by using a Greek word (mataios) that means “useless, vain.” The LXX then translates the Hebrew word ʾākzāb (“deception”) with a second Greek word (kena) that also means “empty,” “vain,” or “worthless.”57 Relatedly, neither Greek word appears elsewhere to translate these Hebrew words. The name of the town thus disappears in the LXX while two Greek synonyms for “vain” appear that are not present in Hebrew: “frivolous houses” and “will become useless to the kings of Israel.” The LXX thus attempts to make sense of the MT and changes the Hebrew text but even these changes still suggest the translator worked from a text that was quite close to the MT we currently possess.

The essential literary unity of 1:8–16 functions within the larger whole (1:2–16), as noted at the beginning of 1:2–7. The unit transitions from the prophet’s own lament (1:8–9) to an admonition to various groups in the Shephelah (1:10–16) in response to the theophany (1:3–4) and the pronouncement of judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem (1:5–7).58 Generally, these admonitions concern actions that various cities and fortified towns should take or not take in response to the forthcoming judgment of Judah and Jerusalem. Some town names are the names of actual towns or small fortified villages in Philistia (e.g., Gath in 1:10), in the Shephelah (e.g., Lachish in 1:13), or Judah (Jerusalem in 1:12) whose exact location may or may not be known (perhaps, Achzib in 1:14). Most of the sayings, however, involve word plays on the names of towns, but they do not use the actual names of the town. In these cases, the towns are real, but the names used in the speech subtly participate in admonishing these places for their own guilt even while focusing primarily upon the impending punishment of Judah and Jerusalem. A considerable number of scholars interpret the threat to these sites as anticipating the events of 701 BCE when Sennacherib laid siege to Jerusalem. Several scholars also argue that short comments in 1:9, 12 reflect exilic theological interpretations intended to strengthen the implications that Jerusalem’s deliverance from Sennacherib ultimately did not prevent the people of Jerusalem from returning to the worship of other deities.59 These exilic interpretations stress that the prophet warns Jerusalem they will be punished eventually for the worship of other deities. For most of these scholars these theologically driven comments presuppose knowledge that Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon in 587 and intentionally evoke the events of 587 as well as 701 BCE. Thus, the prophetic warnings presuppose a paradigm of history that implies Yahweh has repeatedly warned Israel and Judah by communicating the divine word through Yahweh’s servants the prophets. These later texts connect Micah’s warnings both to events at the end of the eighth century and to the eventual destruction of Jerusalem at the beginning of the sixth century. In this sense, these exilic additions function as proleptic statements from the time of the prophet just before 701 BCE, even though their insertion into the text probably did not occur until after 587 BCE.

These exilic additions are often (but not always) paired with 1:5–7 (or portions thereof) as a means of creating a literary foreshadowing that anticipates the climactic pronunciation of the destruction of Jerusalem in Mic 3:12.60 As such, they help to anchor 1:10–16 into the thematic development of 1:3–7. In other words, an early source associated with Sennacherib’s attacks (most of 1:10–16 and at least some portion of 1:8–9) was updated to highlight the prophecy associated with Micah’s message of future judgment (which did not happen in 701 BCE, but ultimately came to pass in 587 BCE). The exilic theological affirmation of the prophetic message shows similarities to the theological explanation of Jerusalem’s destruction as the end of a lengthy process that appears in 2 Kgs 17:34–41.

Micah 1:10–16 returns to the lament theme of 1:8, but the entity being lamented is multivalent. Apart from Gath, scholars have not definitively identified the locations of the villages mentioned. These verses cohere in their final form by means of common style, paronomasia, geographic focus, and rhetorical functions. Stylistically, 1:10 opens the unit with a plural imperative, but the remainder of the unit (1:11–16) largely uses feminine singular imperatives whose subject is “the inhabitant” of various cities (1:11, 12, 13, 15). The paronomasia in these verses creates word plays with either the meaning or the sound of the city names that are mentioned. The geographical focus centers upon Philistine or Judean cities of the Shephelah that suffer under the onslaught of Sennacherib’s military campaigns at the end of the eighth century BCE.61 Further, in general terms, the six towns mentioned in 1:10–12 are usually considered to be further away from Jerusalem than the five towns mentioned in 1:13–16, so the spatial movement implied by these threats implies that the danger increasingly approaches Jerusalem.

The rhetorical function of 1:10–16 is twofold: to pronounce judgment upon the regions taken by the Assyrians and to use that judgment as a warning to Jerusalem that it will soon suffer the same fate (1:12b, 13b). The combination of the two rhetorical purposes has been explained variously. The Jerusalem material, or portions of it, is often treated as a redactional adaptation that serves the same function as the warnings to Jerusalem in 1:5b–7, 9.62 The named villages also appear to be grouped to increase the threat to Jerusalem, since the threats move from Philistia to Jerusalem, implicitly heightening the impending sense of doom.





1. The Prophet’s Own Lament (1:8–9)


8 The prophet speaks in 1:8, as indicated by the first-person singular pronoun, a style that in Micah happens elsewhere only in 3:1, 8 and 7:1–7. The previous verses used first-person speech, but in Mic 1:6–7, Yahweh is the speaker based upon the character of the actions described. In 1:8, the speaker laments while walking barefoot and naked, actions that make clear that Yahweh is not the speaker. Some recent commentators cite this self-reporting speech as setting Micah apart from other eighth-century prophets, but this claim overstates the singularity of the speeches.63 Consequently, many of these scholars emphasize this first-person prophetic account as evidence in dating this speech to the time of Micah, though this criterion alone is not compelling.64 Yet, most scholars adduce additional criteria for including (at least most of) 1:8–9 with this unit as part of the early core of the collection. Two literary observations also lead to the conclusion that 1:8–9 could not have been the original opening of a unit, especially because of the pronouns in these verses that require antecedents. First, this at the beginning of 1:8 must refer to something as the reason for lamentation. No convincing criteria can be marshaled to claim the opening of 1:8 should be read anaphorically (i.e., as referring to something that follows). Rather, in its current form, this refers to Yahweh’s judgment announced back in 1:3–7. In the final form of the text, this most naturally refers to the judgment against Samaria (1:6–7) and the implications that this judgment has for Jerusalem (1:5). Second, the reference to “her” wound in 1:9 refers to Samaria (1:6). The pronominal suffix continues the third-person feminine singular pronouns of 1:7 that also refer to Samaria, since capital cities are often personified as feminine figures.65 While the third-person feminine singular suffixes of 1:9 likely refer to Samaria in 1:7, the I speaker in 1:8 is the prophet while the I who speaks in 1:6–7 is Yahweh. In this sense, too, the prophet’s actions can be interpreted as a response to the judgment announced by Yahweh in 1:3–7.

The prophet who mourns naked and barefoot in 1:8 represents one of several significant parallels in Micah connecting actions or sayings of Micah with those of Isaiah.66 The only other time one finds the combination “naked and barefoot” in the Old Testament is Isa 20:2–4. These verses recount the prophet’s symbolic action of walking in lamentation without clothes or shoes in response to an attack on Philistia by Sargon, the Assyrian king in 711 BCE. These actions were intended as a warning against relying on Philistia or Egypt for help against Assyria. The actions combine mourning and military defeat wherein the soldiers on the losing side are taken away as slaves and humiliated by having to walk into exile without clothing. Isaiah 20:2–4 narrates the events and speaks about the prophet in the third person while the prophet uses a first-person style in Mic 1:8. In 1:8, the prophet Micah speaks of walking naked and barefoot in response to an attack on the coastal region and the Shephelah from Sennacherib in 701 BCE. The lament in Isa 20:1 refers to the city of Ashdod while Mic 1:10 warns Gath. The attack on Ashdod happened in the reign of Sargon in 711 BCE while most scholars interpret the threat in Mic 1:10 as the series of attacks by Sargon’s son Sennacherib in 701 BCE.67 Nevertheless, the similarities are striking, even though the two prophetic writings may presume different events. Micah’s symbolic-action report, delivered in the first person, creates a twin event with the warning of Isaiah a decade earlier, meaning that somehow Micah’s symbolic action mirrors that of Jerusalem’s most famous prophet of the day. The personal style in Micah makes the plaintive actions more evocative since Micah’s actions come with haunting sound effects.

The prophet begins to lament and wail so loudly that his lamentation sounds like the wild animals that inhabit the desolate places. In 1:8b, the prophet wails like howling jackals and screeching ostriches. The significance of these animal sounds conjures the loud, plaintive cries by these animals in particular.68 The fact that these two animals are frequently associated with deserted, nearly uninhabitable lands symbolizes the desolate state of Samaria which, in turn, accentuates the threat against Jerusalem.

9 Micah 1:9 also uses feminine singular pronouns and verbs that relate well to the setting in the book, but careful evaluation indicates that these pronouns refer to two different antecedents. Reference to her wound assumes Samaria as the antecedent, but the third-person feminine singular it refers back to the feminine word wound (makkâ). Literarily, the wound refers to the devastation inflicted upon Samaria that led to its destruction (722 BCE) that was described previously: the destruction of the city’s foundation walls (1:6), along with the smashing and burning of its idols (1:7). In turn, 1:9 functions as part of the prophet’s own symbolic-action report in 1:8. The memory of this prophetic speech portrays a situation that matches with certain findings of the material culture of the late eighth and seventh centuries. Historically, following Hezekiah’s death (696 BCE), the lengthy reign of his son Manasseh (king from 696–641 BCE) saw considerable accommodation to Assyrian overlords, probably both politically and religiously.69 In 2 Kgs 21:5, the Deuteronomistic Historian refers to the altars of “all the host of heaven” that Manasseh installed in the temple precinct and probably alludes obliquely to the astral deities worshiped by the Assyrians. The archaeological record also shows a significant increase in astral symbols among seventh-century seals and other iconography found in Judah, so it seems reasonable to assume that the syncretism described by the Deuteronomistic Historian (2 Kgs 21:3–8), while certainly polemical, likely reflects the memories of the political policies of Manasseh, who sought to remain on good terms with Assyria during his reign.70

Hence, Mic 1:9 draws on the content of 1:5–7 by assuming that Samaria’s destruction was caused by its idolatry and that Jerusalem’s imitation of Samaria’s behavior (like 1:5b) threatens Jerusalem with the same fate as Samaria. The similarity of the perspective of this verse and 1:5b becomes particularly clear in 1:9b. The latter half of 1:9 drives home the point that Samaria’s wound has reached Judah and Jerusalem. This claim sets up an analogy consistent with the theological aims of 2 Kgs 17:7–20, where Samaria’s destruction is narrated and theologized.71 In so doing, Mic 1:9b binds itself to Mic 1:5–7. Quite a number of scholars have described this connection as redactional in nature, meaning that the prophetic lament of 1:8 was not originally associated with a theological interpretation of the fall of Samaria.72 In all likelihood, 1:9 represents a redactional insertion to link the lament of 1:8 with the rhetorical unit of 1:10–16. The fact that the events of Samaria’s destruction (722 BCE) in 1:5–7, 9 also link the prophetic lament of 1:8, 10–16 (reflecting the events of 701 BCE) further enhances the idea that the theologizing of 1:9 reflects a periodization of the last two decades of the eighth century to convey theological ideas noticeably found in 2 Kgs 17:7–20.





2. Warning to the Shephelah and Jerusalem (1:10–16)


10 Micah 1:10 mentions two villages, but only one of them can be identified confidently. The village of Gath was located about twenty-three miles west of Jerusalem on the western edge of Judean territory known as the Shephelah. At times, Gath belongs to the Philistines, but at the end of the eighth century, it belonged to Judah prior to the Assyrian invasion. The best guess for the location of Beth-Leaphrah was a village on the eastern edge of the Shephelah located just under twenty miles from Jerusalem.73

Interestingly, the admonitions of 1:10–16 begin with what most recognize as a citation of 2 Sam 1:20:

2 Sam 1:20

Mic 1:10



Tell it not in Gath,

Do not declare it in Gath;



proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon;

Do not weep in



or the daughters of the Philistines will rejoice,

Beth-Leaphrah.



the daughters of the uncircumcised will exult.

Roll around in the dust.



The contexts of the two passages are quite different, but those differences add to the poignancy of the confrontation in Micah. The command in 2 Sam 1:20 reflects David’s response to the news of Saul’s death at the hands of the Philistines, and the parallel line that refers to Ashkelon indicates that the text of 2 Sam 1:20 presupposes that Gath was considered Philistine territory at the time. By contrast, Gath and its daughter cities such as Moresheth-Gath (Mic 1:1, 14) were part of Judah in the eighth century BCE. While the second half of 2 Sam 1:20 mentions the Philistines, the verb in the second line in Mic 10 uses the verb plš (roll around), meaning it uses the same three consonants as Philistia (Heb. pəlešet). One can thus readily see 1:10bβ as an echo of the Philistines in 2 Sam 1:20. By evoking the language of 2 Sam 1:20, Mic 1:10 indicates the powerful and foreboding significance of the commands. The death of Saul in 2 Sam 1:20 officially marks the beginning of the reign of David, and Mic 1:10–16 (esp. with the pronouncements against Jerusalem in 1:12, 13) threatens the city of Jerusalem and with it, the Davidic monarchy. Relatedly, the name of the town Beth-Leaphrah literally means “house of dust,” using the same word as in the command to roll around in dust that ends 1:10. The command in the last line thus conveys wordplays with the name house of dust and Philistia. Implicitly, Jerusalem’s punishment also threatens the Philistines.

11 The exact location of Shaphir remains unknown, but it was presumably a small town in the Shephelah since the next several locations specify the inhabitant of the city using the feminine singular construct form to express the collective city population.74 The prophet’s call to lament continues, again using a pun between the name of this town and its fate. The Aramaic and Hebrew root špr means “to be beautiful.” Remembering that the names in 1:10–16 represent cities, one quickly sees that the city named beautiful becomes nakedness and shame, essentially conveying the idea that the beautiful city has been stripped bare. Persons taken in the aftermath of battles could be forced to march naked as a means of humiliation, but the description in 1:11 makes more sense as a reference to the city’s devastation. The MT is cryptic, but it does make sense. The feminine imperative that opens the verse aligns with the feminine singular word inhabitant, though the next word addresses the audience using a second-person masculine plural object on the l preposition. Elsewhere, the imperative of ʿbr followed by the l preposition emphasizes the command to those who receive it: Pass through for yourselves (Deut 2:13; Josh 22:19). Since inhabitant represents the collective whole, reversion to the more common plural form is not unprecedented. The command essentially means, “See for yourselves, inhabitant of Shaphir, the shameful nakedness.” The statement assumes that the city has been razed. The shaming of cities personified as women who are stripped represents a motif in other texts to depict the destruction of the main city (e.g., Lady Nineveh in Nah 3:4–7; personified Jerusalem in Ezek 16:6–39; or Lady Edom in Lam 4:21).

The next syntactical clause refers to the town Zenaan that also cannot be confidently located to a specific place and appears only in this verse.75 The wordplay on this village functions more subtly than many of the other puns. The paronomasia relates both to the sound of Zenaan when spoken and the irony created with the verb yāṣʾa, a verbal root that means go forth. The verb appears with the particle of negation to describe the consequences of the military campaign: the inhabitant of the town will not go forth (yāṣʾa).76 In other words, the inhabitant of the town whose-name-sounds-like-go-forth shall not go forth, because she cannot do so. The city will be destroyed.

The term house of Azel (bêt hāʾēṣel) also does not appear elsewhere in the Old Testament; nor has a specific site for the village been identified. Because the names of the other cities in this passage involve word plays, several scholars suggest interpretations that involve a word play with one of three verbs derived from the consonants ʾṣl. Scholars most commonly suggest the root ʾēṣel II, which can mean “take back,” “remove,” or “withhold.”77 A few mention Wolfram von Soden’s suggestion that the name plays off the Hebrew word ṣēl (“shadow” or “protection”) that is prefixed with an aleph of negation.78 They treat the name as a taunt to Assyria, understanding the name to mean “house-of-no-protection.” They do not, however, offer good explanations for the Hebrew word ʿemdâ (“support,” “standing place”) at the end of the line. Hence, the phraseology of Mic 1:11b reflects the rhetorical aims of 1:10–16.

12 The village named in 1:12 cannot be located, and the paronomasia associated with it likely plays off the meaning of the village name rather than the sound. The name Maroth essentially means “bitter things.” The description in 1:12a describes the inhabitant of the village with the unusual phrase writhing for good. Unfortunately, most English versions translate the verb benignly as “wait.” In so doing, they mistakenly downplay the pain associated with the description, since the verb used here implies contortion. The verb can be used to refer to “dance” but it also appears in contexts where one “writhes” in pain (e.g., such as in birth pangs associated with labor). To be sure, good should be interpreted substantively as the opposite of bitterness, and thus the wordplay effectively creates a tragic scene where bitter things hope for good, thereby inverting the name of the village. Sadly, good will not come. Micah 1:12b indicates that rāʿ (“evil,” “calamity”) from Yahweh has descended upon the city, which simultaneously means any hope for good has become futile. The phrase thus conveys a kind of ambiguous double entendre. When first heard, 1:12a could sound like the inhabitant is rejoicing (i.e., “dancing for good”), but with the continuation in 1:12b the reader/hearer must understand the verb to mean “contorting in pain” because evil has arrived at the gate of Jerusalem.

Micah 1:10–12 thus mentions six towns that are the focus of Yahweh’s destruction. Together they imply an impending attack on Jerusalem. This subsection ends with two kî clauses in 1:12, essentially mirroring the two kî clauses from 1:9 that also speak of the impending threat (incurable wound) that has found its way to the gate of Jerusalem.

Several scholars treat 1:12b as a later insertion that links up with the desire to portray Jerusalem’s fate in terms parallel to that of Samaria.79 Two observations point in the direction of 1:12b stemming from a later hand. First, as already noted, the shared theme with other sections of Mic 1–3 of Jerusalem following the path of Samaria connects well with 1:5–7, 13b. Second, 1:12b contains the only third-person reference to Yahweh in 1:10–16, a characteristic that sets 1:12b apart from the remainder of the deity’s speech in 1:15. Nevertheless, most assess 1:12b as part of the core composition based upon two observations.80 First, and most important, without 1:12b the brief statement about the village Maroth contains no explanation for its writhing, thereby greatly weakening the pun on the name of the city (as well as the message of judgment). Second, if 1:12b represents an insertion, then one would expect that 1:12a would have originally continued with 1:13. Yet, 1:12a makes little sense when read directly with 1:13. Consequently, when one recognizes that 1:10–16 in its earliest form already focused on an impending threat to Jerusalem, then 1:12b (and 1:9) need not have been originally tied to the fate of Samaria as in 1:5–7, 13b. The dominant message of 1:9–12 warns of an enemy that destroys towns in the Shephelah. It likely evokes the threat of Sennacherib’s campaign in 701 BCE.

13 In 1:13–16, the focus shifts to the destruction of Lachish (and likely the fortified towns surrounding it). Lachish was a significant and strategic military center in Judah. It was a fortified city (according to 2 Chr 11:9, one of several established by Rehoboam after the breakup of the united monarchy) whose destruction in 701 BCE signaled the grave danger facing Jerusalem from the Assyrian Empire. The destruction of Lachish represented such a significant victory for Sennacherib that he memorialized its defeat in a series of reliefs on the walls of his temple.81 The town was just under thirty miles from Jerusalem and Mic 1:13 hints at the military significance of Lachish by calling for the city to prepare for battle by hitching the chariots to the warhorses.

The second half of 1:13 has been treated as a secondary insertion by several commentators because of its thematic similarities with 1:5–7 where Jerusalem is threatened with punishment because it followed the sins of Samaria.82 Unlike 1:12b, Mic 1:13b explicitly connects Jerusalem (Lady Zion) with the rebellions of Israel, making the arguments for its later inclusion with 1:5–7, 9b more compelling than was the case with 1:12b.83 What is not clear is the situation behind the allusion to Lachish being the beginning of sin for Zion in 1:13bα. The phrasing appears to imply that Lachish sinned and somehow her behavior has been adopted by Jerusalem in a manner that now threatens Jerusalem. In this sense, the link between 1:13b and 1:5, 9b does not flow as clearly as many have presumed at first glance. It is possible that 1:13bα existed as part of the core text and had military connotations, while only 1:13bβ was inserted to connect back to the Samaria parallel theme. The parallelism, however, makes it more likely that the two versets belong together. Explanations for 1:13b have included at least four factors. Leslie Allen sees the charge as the repetition of the condemnation of the sins and rebellion of 1:5, but with a military focus on Lachish. He also connects 1:13b with reliance upon military might as in 5:10(9) as one of the “false mainstays” of Judah.84 Jeremias correctly notes that the imagery used here is unusual since the condemnation of the chariots of Lachish symbolizes both the guilt of Jerusalem and the already destroyed Northern Kingdom.85 He also notes the thematic connection to the later text in 5:9–13 where the condemnation of Judah’s reliance upon military strength rather than reliance upon Yahweh plays a significant role. Jeremias does not, however, suggest that 1:13 comes from the same hand as 5:9–13.86 Marvin Sweeney focuses upon the assonance between Lachish and the Hebrew word for “steeds” (rekeš) to explain the unusual language.87 He treats the sin/transgression language as referring to an act of revolt against Assyria by Lachish that is parallel to the rebellion that had caused Samaria’s destruction.
