Wolff, interestingly, argues that the reference to chariots and steeds here cannot refer to battle preparations because of the context, but that this imagery likely refers to the spoils that the Assyrian army took. He refers to the list of items taken by Sargon II that included the number of horses and chariots that he confiscated after defeating Samaria when he claimed to have taken captive “27,280 people and their chariots.”88 Simultaneously, Wolff assigns 1:13b to a Deuteronomistic commentator, and argues that 1:13b represents a theological interpretation of the events that exhibits a didactic style. He interprets the word “first” qualitatively rather than chronologically. In other words, Wolff understands rēʾšît as implying the apex or “chief” sin rather than the “first” in a series.89

14 The metaphors and paronomasia in 1:14 essentially combine to portray the divorce of Moresheth-Gath, the prophet’s hometown (1:1). The word translated as parting gift does not imply a gesture of hospitality, but the payment of a dowry by the father of the bride that must be returned if divorce occurs. Both aspects of this term are documentable in biblical texts. In 1 Kgs 9:16 the pharaoh gave the Philistine city of Gezer as a dowry when Solomon married his daughter. Exodus 18:2 indicates that Moses gave Jethro his parting gifts back to him when he sent Zipporah and their two sons back to Jethro. Thus, parting gifts represent the beginning or the end of a marriage. In Mic 1:14, the context demands that the reader understand that a relationship is ending. The command is delivered to a feminine entity, most likely assumed to be Lady Zion who is mentioned in 1:13. Moresheth-Gath would have been understood as one of the satellite cities of Jerusalem, and this appears to be the relationship that is dissolving in 1:13.

The last half of 1:14 uses a pun to convey judgment and betrayal on Achzib, a village roughly nineteen miles from Jerusalem. The name of the town, Achzib, creates a pun with the announcement that its houses will become a deception (ʾākzāb), a word that sounds very much like Achzib. Some have argued that the village was a site of pottery and linen workshops, possibly the place where potters produced the famous lmlk jars.90 The verse announces the loss of the houses of Achzib to the kings of Israel. If, as seems plausible, the houses refer to production centers that produced the lmlk jars and other commodities, which were used to collect taxes for the monarchy, then this verse makes sense as another example of a prophetic interpretation of the implications of the Assyrian invasion. The reference to the kings of Israel here, as is often noted, refers to the kings of Judah. This reference appears consistent with the use of Israel to refer to Judah in Mic 1:15; 3:1, 8–9.

15 In 1:15, two versets form an intricate poetic line held together by semantic parallels and by a logical cause-and-effect relationship. The semantic parallels are marked by two different words that begin each verset that have the same consonants (ʿd), but different vowels. The verse begins with again (ʿōd) while Mic 1:15b begins with the preposition to (ʿad). The semantic parallels continue since each half of the verse contains the verb bôʾ, but the two different instances of the verb reflect action from opposing directions of the same verb (bôʾ can mean both “to come/bring” and “to go”). In 1:15a, the speaker uses bôʾ to announce the coming of the oppressor, while 1:15b utilizes bôʾ to announce the departure of Judah’s king. The first half of the verse implies a military threat when it refers to the one possessing. This conqueror will come while the one who is called the glory of Israel will depart for Adullam. The latter half thus refers to the king as the glory and it does so by referring to the fortified city of Adullam. Adullam is generally interpreted as an oblique allusion to the place of refuge where David hid in a cave when fleeing from Saul (1 Sam 22:1).

The verse continues to address the same feminine singular entity as in 1:13–14, the personified city. The speaker changes, however, since the first-person speech claims to perform an action that only a deity could claim, namely the sending of an oppressor to punish the kingdom. This divine pronouncement sets these verses apart from 1:8–9, where the first-person speaker has to be understood as the prophet himself. It also sets 1:15 apart formally from 1:12, where Yahweh appears in the third person. These two variations in speakers cannot be easily reconciled formally, but they can be explained by the fact that the prophetic speeches switch between the voice of the prophet and the voice of Yahweh with some regularity. This same alternation already occurs in Micah since the call to attention and the theophany description in Mic 1:2–4 refer to Yahweh in the third person while 1:6 also uses first-person verbs that must be associated with divine speech. Also, 2:3 presents both forms of reference: the messenger formula that begins the verse refers to Yahweh in the third person, while the quoted speech of Yahweh uses first-person forms. Hence, the change of speaker to the divine speech form in 1:15 does not appear definitive for determining the homogeneity of the unit.

16 The addressee remains the personified city in 1:16 as indicated by three feminine singular imperative verb forms (cut, shave, enlarge) and three second-person feminine singular pronominal suffixes (your). The city is commanded to debase herself in shame and lamentation by cutting off her hair and shaving herself bald. The reason for this command must be inferred from the two halves of the verse. The first half refers to the children of your luxury as the reason for these actions, but it does not indicate whether their actions or their fate should be the cause of her lamentation. The second half of the verse refers to these same children as having been exiled from her. In this sense, then, clearly the fate of the children (i.e., her people) provides cause for the lament. Yet, if one takes account of 1:10–15* as the context for this statement, then one must also recognize that the exile was not unprovoked from Yahweh’s perspective. In the final form of the text, Jerusalem is condemned both for its military actions (1:13) and its idolatry (1:7), though a strong case can be made that the latter emphasis entered only with the compilation of Mic 1–3, while the military critique played the central role in 1:10–16* before it was joined with the other portions of Mic 1–3.

Micah 1 thus shows signs of an editorial hand that has combined preexisting material for rhetorical purposes. Following a superscription (1:1) that sets Micah at the end of the eighth century BCE, the chapter begins with a call to attention. A description of a theophany (1:2–4) then announces Yahweh’s appearance for judgment. The reason for that judgment is provided by 1:5–7, namely Judah’s refusal to turn from the religious practices for which Samaria had also been condemned. The prophetic response (1:8–9) of lamentation leads to proclamation of the implications of this judgment that includes the destruction of population centers in the Shephelah as the oppressor moves toward Jerusalem in 1:10–16. These poetic images thus evoke the broad outlines of the military campaigns of Sennacherib at the end of the eighth century BCE when Judah effectively became a vassal state of Assyria. While the Assyrians did not totally destroy Jerusalem, its fortified towns and its territory were largely destroyed, leaving it with little choice but to acquiesce to Assyrian fealty demands. While Judah’s king remained on the throne, in all other respects it essentially answered to Assyria for the better part of the next century and its territory was greatly diminished.

Communities of faith today both resonate with and express discomfort with the theological statements and portraits of God present in Mic 1. Christian and Jewish communities of faith instinctively wish to affirm the rejection of the worship of idols that appears so prominently in 1:5–7. They often echo their appreciation of a portrait of God that is big enough to act against political powers that might threaten us. At the same time, the violence of Yahweh’s actions frightens us. We speak blithely in prayers, asking Yahweh to come down to us. The theophany language in Mic 1 represents a very different response to the appearance of Yahweh in the world. Yahweh, the warrior king, descends to the earth to punish those doing wrong. Creation cannot hold Yahweh, and so mountains collapse. Yahweh cannot overlook the worship of other deities by those professing to worship him, so Yahweh decides to destroy their land, their cities, and their people. Some are so repulsed by the violence that they reject the message altogether. Others try to explain it as the way that Yahweh acted prior to the coming of Jesus, who offered a kinder, gentler portrait of God. These claims ignore the fact that while some New Testament texts speak powerfully about God’s grace, other New Testament texts speak just as powerfully about the violent punishment God will inflict upon those who get in his way. Conversely, the Old Testament contains numerous passages regarding God’s grace that would compare favorably to the claims about grace in New Testament texts. Hosea 11 and Mic 4:1–4 represent grand visions of divine grace and a call to all nations to come and worship in Jerusalem.

Micah 1:10–16 threatens Jerusalem with divine destruction by a foreign enemy used by Yahweh. In today’s world, wars and rumors of war are rampant. The text uses agricultural imagery to speak about military devastation. Now, however, today’s human armies literally have the power to level cities so that they become bumps in the field, as the images of the destruction of the cities of Ukraine make clear. Christian churches and practitioners become targets of mass killings and brutal murder, not because they are practicing idolatry, but because they are trying to be faithful to their own Christian and Jewish theological commitments. To whom do these communities turn?

At the same time, very few Christian or Jewish communities of faith would claim that they worship idols. Such responses help us to “other” the message of prophetic texts like Mic 1. The things that keep us resistant to the worship of God are not technically idols, so we let ourselves off the hook. At the same time, we do not have any difficulty naming the worship practices of other religions as idolatrous. Protestants, in some circles, express concern about the presence of priests in worship and bemoan the practice of rituals with which they are not familiar. Too often, we want to label the genuine theological commitments of others as heresy. We may express doubt that we have lived up to all that God expects from us, but we are quick to condemn others for their shortcomings.

All of these diverse reactions have a certain amount of truth to them. Interpreting biblical texts remains a complicated endeavor, especially since the authors and editors who created these texts also make such diverse theological claims within and across theological books. In this respect, the juxtaposed truth claims in prophetic books structure themselves to move between judgment and grace, between justice as punishment and a hope for justice from oppressors. Prophetic books routinely stress judgment in the opening chapters and end with words of hope for Yahweh’s people. The book of Amos, for example, offers not a single word of hope that Israel will escape Yahweh’s punishment for almost the entire book (1:1–9:6), but the book concludes with two short speeches of hope in which Yahweh offers hope that a small remnant will survive (9:7–10) and that restoration of the kingdom will restore the ruined cities and lead to a fertility of the land, the likes of which have no parallel (9:11–15). Likewise, Mic 1–3 culminates with the pronouncement that Jerusalem will be plowed under by the divine farmer and left to lie fallow (3:12). The very next verse begins a unit (4:1–4) that calls upon the nations to come to Jerusalem when the mountain of Yahweh’s house will be the highest mountain and nations will stream to it to learn Yahweh’s ways and Yahweh’s instruction (tōrâ) so that all may live in peace. The nations will beat their swords into plowshares and turn their knives into pruning hooks. These verses echo the words of Isa 2:2–4 almost verbatim. Micah 7 also ends with an affirmation of Yahweh’s grace and forgiveness (7:18–20). These recurring combinations of judgment followed by grace provide most prophetic books within the Book of the Twelve and the Book of the Twelve as a whole with a trajectory of grace tempered with dramatic calls to remain accountable by honoring God’s covenant and ethical expectations. This trajectory of hope should be borne in mind as we read the prophetic books and think about the world in which we live.





1. Despite the wide variety of compositional models represented, the number of scholars suggesting that multiple hands have shaped the superscription has grown markedly in recent decades. See Ina Willi-Plein, Vorformen der Schriftexegese innerhalb des Alten Testaments: Untersuchungen zum literarischen Werden der auf Amos, Hosea und Micha zurückgehenden Bücher im hebräischen Zwölfprophetenbuch, BZAW 123 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1971), 70; Theodor Lescow, “Redaktionsgeschichtliche Analyse von Micha 1–5,” ZAW 84 (1972): 62, DOI: 10.1515/zatw.1972.84.1.46; Jeremias, 125–27; Jeremias, “Die Deutung der Gerichtsworte Michas in der Exilszeit,” ZAW 83 (1971): 352–53, DOI: 10.1515/zatw.1971.83.3.330; Wilhelm Rudolph, Micha, Nahum, Habakuk, Zephanja: Mit einer Zeittafel von Alfred Jepsen, KAT 13 (Gütersloh: Mohn, 1975), 31; Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 127–28; Schart, Die Entstehung, 40–46; Jakob Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen des Zwölfprophetenbuches: Entstehung und Komposition, BZAW 360 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2006), 33–39. The three kings in Mic 1:1 reflect a retrospective summary of Micah’s ministry that is consistent with the so-called Deuteronomistic style of superscriptions, and the thematic summary at the end of 1:1 anticipates 1:5–7, 9a, 12b, all of which appear to call Judah’s leaders to learn a lesson from Samaria’s destruction.

2. Some (e.g., Willi-Plein, Vorformen, 70–72) have understood the opening unit (following the superscription) to include 1:2–9, while others argue that the opening composition included significant portions of 1:2–16 (e.g., Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 139–46). They treat 1:2–7 as a part of a larger whole.

3. E.g., see Mays, 38. He describes the verses as having thematic continuity while at the same time classifying the parts as independent sayings. He argues that both roles need to be considered.

4. Consider three examples. Smith (16–18) reports a number of scholars who question the originality of certain verses, but then simply assumes 1:2–7 is the work of the prophet because he sees no “compelling reason” (17, emphasis mine) to deny Micah is the author. Mays (13, 42) argues that 1:3–5a represents an original oracle from the prophet while 1:2 and 1:5b–7 represent the work of the redaction of ch. 1 when chs. 1–3 were first combined into a collection. Jeremias, by contrast, sees 1:3–7 as an exilic text that was composed as the introduction to Mic 1–3 and was added when Micah expanded in the Persian period to include Mic 1–5 while 1:2, with its antagonism against the nations, enters as part of the final redaction in the Hellenistic period. Jörg Jeremias, Die Propheten Joel, Obadja, Jona, Micha, ATD 24.3 (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2007), 116, 120, 132–33.

5. E.g., Schart, Die Entstehung, 177; and Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 139–40. Schart maintains that only 1:2a should be seen as secondary, while Wöhrle treats the entire verse as a later addition.

6. Jeremias, 131–32; Schart, Die Entstehung, 177; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 139–40. Schart sees 1:2–7 as a developing introduction that grew in three stages (Schart, Die Entstehung, 177–83). For him, Mic 1:2a entered with 1:1 and 1:5b during the exilic period, while the early core of the first unit (containing 1:2b, 5a, 6–7) only concerned Samaria. For Schart, 1:3–4 represents a later insertion into the exilic D Korpus that also added other creation-themed insertions into the Book of the Four (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Zephaniah). Wöhrle also believes he can isolate three layers of material in Mic 1:2–16, but he describes these layers differently (Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 139–40). He sees 1:2, in its entirety, as a late addition to the introduction. The reason for inserting 1:2 was to presage a major redactional expansion concerning judgment on the nations (a layer he calls the “foreign nations layer I” or “Fremdvölkerschicht I” that transcends a number of writings in the Book of the Twelve). Jeremias (131) argues that Mic 1 has grown from back to front, so that 1:8–9 was added as a bridge between the early composition of 1:10–16 and the first introduction to the book (1:3–7), one that was created before the addition of chs. 4–5 (132). Then, according to Jeremias, 1:2 forms a frame with 5:15 when chs. 4–5 were added to chs. 1–3 because only with chs. 4–5 does one find the theme of judgment on the nations. He argues that 1:3–7 represents an exilic introduction to Mic 1–3 that uses Hosea and Amos to set up the admonition of Jerusalem through the example of Samaria.

7. The relationship of chs. 6–7 and 4–5 with Mic 1–3 is a complex question. See the treatment of the development of Micah in the introduction to this commentary.

8. The Tetragrammaton refers to the four consonants (yhwh) that comprise the divine name Yahweh, whose meaning is a third-person declaration, “he is” or “he will be” or even “he will cause to be.” It is important to remember that Yahweh functions as a name, not a title. The Greek word kyrios means Lord and appears to reflect the sense that the Tetragrammaton was too holy to pronounce in public. Biblical writers of the Hebrew Bible, however, did not shy away from using the name of God.

9. See Rainer Albertz and Rüdiger Schmitt, Family and Household Religion in Ancient Israel and the Levant (Winona Lake, IN: Eisenbrauns, 2012), 248–52.

10. See the recent contribution to the ongoing discussion by Oded Lipschits and Jakob Wöhrle, “Azekah—the Hometown of Micah the Moreshtite,” ZAW 135 (2023): 230–50. They show how ideas concerning the location of the prophet’s home were unduly influenced by Christian sources from a much later time, and they reinvigorate the suggestion of identifying Moresheth-Gath with Azekah, a village that existed in the Bronze Age, but that passed into Judean hands toward the end of the ninth century BCE.

11. E.g., Wolff thinks that most speeches in chs. 1–2 were delivered in Moresheth-Gath while ch. 3 was delivered in Jerusalem. Hans Walter Wolff, Micah: A Commentary, trans. Gary Stansell, CC (Minneapolis: Augsburg, 1990), 6. He believes Micah was an elder in the hill country village who challenges the rulers (2:1–2, 3–4), prophets (3:5–7), and leaders of Jerusalem (3:1, 9–11).

12. Baruch’s scribal role extended well beyond his ability to transcribe speeches. He was a member of the family of Shaphan. He was well connected with important priestly and scribal families in the late seventh and early sixth centuries BCE. Baruch was the descendant of Hilkiah, the priest who had worked with Hezekiah. Shaphan was the royal scribe to whom the book of the covenant (Deuteronomy) was given when it was found by the priest repairing the temple in the time of Josiah. Shaphan’s grandson was Gedaliah who was appointed governor of Judah by the Babylonians. Another one of Shaphan’s sons, Elasah, we are told, takes a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles in Babylon (Jer 29:3). Gemariah, son of Shaphan, was present when Jeremiah’s scroll was read before Jehoiakim (Jer 36:11–14). Clearly, the Shaphanides were a significant family in the political world of Judah in the late seventh century BCE, and Jeremiah was allied with this family.

13. The vast majority of critical scholars since the beginning of the twentieth century confine material from the eighth century BCE only to Mic 1–3. See the discussion in Wolff, 17–27, esp. 26–27; Jeremias, 115–21.

14. The material from Mic 1–3 that most likely refers to eighth-century events covers the fall of Samaria (722 BCE) to the siege of Sennacherib (701 BCE). Micah 1:5b–7 allude to Samaria’s destruction. The villages mentioned in 1:10–17 warn of military encroachment, and most associate the verses with the advances of Sennacherib in 701 BCE. By contrast, the bulk of Mic 2–3 condemns problems that are internal to Judah that reflect actions taken by Hezekiah in the buildup to fortify the land against Assyria prior to 701. See the discussion of the date of the prophet in the introduction to this commentary.

15. See Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 85–89, 127–28; Schart, Die Entstehung, 42–46.

16. Schart suggests this happened in multiple stages with Hosea and Amos being joined earlier and Micah and Zephaniah added later (Schart, Die Entstehung, 45–46, 48–49). In his favor, Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1 spell Hezekiah in ways that are otherwise almost unique in the rest of the Old Testament. This spelling distinguishes Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1 from the spelling of Hezekiah used in Zeph 1:1. Hezekiah has four different spellings in the Old Testament. The majority of the 131 times that the name Hezekiah appears in the Old Testament it is spelled ḥizqiyyāhû (74 times) while 41 times it appears as yĕḥizqiyyāhû (mostly in Chronicles). It appears 13 times with the spelling ḥizqiyyâ (including Zeph 1:1), while it only appears 3 times as yĕḥizqiyyā (Mic 1:1; Hos 1:1; and Ezra 2:16).

17. See Steck, Theological Witness, 43–65; and Seitz, “How Is the Prophet Isaiah Present,” 219–40.

18. See the discussion of the growth of the Micah corpus in the introduction to Micah in this commentary.

19. Scholars have not achieved consensus regarding whether Mic 1:1 is composite and if so, which parts are the earliest. Consider the following examples as illustrative: Schart, Die Entstehung, 39–46; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 37–38, 138–39; Rudolph, 31; Wolff, 33; and Jeremias, 125–27; Lescow, “Redaktionsgeschichtliche Analyse von Micha 1–5,” 61–64; Willi-Plein, Vorformen, 70.

20. Alfred Rahlfs and Robert Hanhart, eds., Septuaginta: Id est Vetus Testamentum graece iuxta LXX interpretes (Stuttgart: Deutsches Bibelgesellschaft, 2006), 512; Ziegler, Duodecim prophetae.

21. See the long list of commentators in Smith-Christopher, 51–53; and those listed in Wolff, 45–46. See also Utzschneider, 32–33.

22. E.g., Utzschneider, 33–34; Artur Weiser, Das Buch der zwölf kleinen Propheten I: Die Propheten Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadja, Jona, Micha, ATD 24 (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1949), 235; Terence E. Fretheim, Reading Hosea–Micah: A Literary and Theological Commentary, Reading the Old Testament (Macon, GA: Smyth & Helwys, 2013), 193–94; Gary Stansell, Micah and Isaiah: A Form and Tradition Historical Comparison, SBLDS 85 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1988), 23, 34.

23. E.g., Smith, 16–17; Allen, 267–68; Smith-Christopher, 52.

24. Jeremias, 132–33; Schart, Die Entstehung, 177–78; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 139–40.

25. So Bernhard Stade, “Streiflichter auf die Entstehung der jetzigen Gestalt der alttestamentlichen Prophetenschriften,” ZAW 23 (1903): 163, DOI: 10.1515/zatw.1903.23.1.153.; and Wolff, 46, who sees the theophany report of 1:3–4 as the insertion of a universalistic editor of Micah.

26. Schart, Die Entstehung, 177, 238–39. So also Stade, “Streiflichter auf die Entstehung,” 163; and Wolff, 46. Schart maintains that Mic 1:3–4 is a theophany that contains two citations of Amos 4:13, the first of three doxologies in Amos (see also 5:8–9 and 9:5–6). These citations include two phrases shared by this hymnic doxology in Amos: “for behold” and “tread upon the high places of the earth.” Schart argues that the high places mentioned in 1:3 are closely associated with 1:5b, but are distinct from the treatment of Zion in Mic 3:12. Relatedly, Mic 1:4 also contains wording that has verbal or thematic links to Amos 9:5–6 (which is recognized by many as an exilic insertion) and to Amos 1:2. Schart does not think that the high places in Mic 1:3, 5b makes sense as a related text, since the shattering of the high places mentioned in the theophany is not tied to 3:12. Micah 3:12 portrays Jerusalem as returning to nature after its destruction. By contrast, 1:5b fits well with 1:3 and the treading upon the high places of the earth.

27. Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 140.

28. Wolff includes Isa 34:1–6 (all the nations in 34:2; Edom in 34:5–6); 51:4–5 (the peoples); Jer 31:10 (deliverance of Israel); and Jer 25:30–31 (where a lawsuit against the nations precedes a theophany report).

29. See J. T. Willis, “Some Suggestions on the Interpretation of Micah 1:2,” VT 18 (1968): 372–79. Willis notes the idiom appears only in contexts where someone accuses another of a violation. There is, thus, no reason to treat Mic 1:2 differently.

30. Nogalski, Literary Precursors, 130, 140–41.

31. E.g., Utzschneider, 32; Theodore H. Robinson, Die Zwölf kleine Propheten, 2nd ed., HAT 14 (Tübingen: Mohr [Siebeck], 1954), 130–31.

32. E.g., Weiser, 232; Jeremias, 133. These commentators argue that 1:2 was added when chs. 4–5 were added to Micah after the exile. For them, 1:2 essentially foreshadows the material dealing with the judgment of Assyria and other nations that appears in those later chapters. Jeremias believes this was done when Micah was part of the Book of the Twelve. The judgment against Jerusalem in Mic 1–3 functions meaningfully within the larger thematic development of the Book of the Four (together with Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah), but the thematic expansion to include judgment on the nations who took advantage of Judah coincides well with the expansions of other books. Jeremias correctly situates this thematic change with later writings of the Twelve. It is also significant that Mic 4–5 represents the beginning of the second half of the Twelve (see the marginal note in Mic 3:12 in the MT).

33. E.g., Smith-Christopher, 52; Smith, 16; Andersen and Freedman, 146–48, 157; Juan I. Alfaro, Micah: Justice and Mercy, ITC (Grand Rapids, Eerdmans, 1989), 13. Despite the fact that they ascribe the verse to the prophet, these commentators describe the change between 1:2 and 1:3–7 very differently from one another. Smith-Christopher explains the change between 1:2 and 1:3 as the result of the transcription of the prophet’s speech and imagines him gesturing with his hands toward the nations. Smith, by contrast, categorically denies that the change in topic has any relationship to the question of Micah’s authorship. Alfaro treats the change of topic as a description of one universal judgment at the end of days that will affect nature, the nations, Samaria, and Judah. Alfaro’s position stands at odds with most understandings of Old Testament eschatology. By contrast, Andersen and Freedman see the change as an essential part of the dispute by interpreting 1:2–4 as part of a theophany report.

34. This happens with some regularity in Hebrew, especially with double vocatives. See GKC §144p.

35. See the translation notes above to explain the different pronunciations of the unpointed text wyhy. For recent commentators who ignore the jussive pointing of the MT, see Fretheim, 194; and Utzschneider, 32. Fretheim treats Yahweh’s appearance as the reason the nations should listen. Utzschneider assumes that the Hebrew word kî introduces a new sentence, not a dependent clause to continue the previous line.

36. So Wilhelm Nowack, “Bemerkungen über das Buch Micha,” ZAW 4 (1884): 288–89.

37. Willis, “Some Suggestions on the Interpretation of Mic 1:2,” 377.

38. Willis, “Some Suggestions on the Interpretation of Mic 1:2,” 375–78. While his evidence that the phrase hyh … lʿd … b elsewhere means “witness against” remains compelling, his interpretation of the trial against the nations for all of 1:2–9 is less successful in explaining the trial dynamics. See the commentary below on 1:5.

39. See Jörg Jeremias, “Theophany in the OT,” IDBSup, 897–98. Jeremias notes that theophany reports presuppose the image of Yahweh as a warrior who comes to battle his enemies. In the Torah, these reports describe action in the past, but in prophetic literature, theophanic reports describe future events (Mic 1:2–7; Amos 1:2) where judgment is directed against Israel or the nations. Jeremias connects this move to the beginning of apocalypticism in the postexilic period.

40. Theodore Hiebert, “Theophany in the OT,” ABD 6:510.

41. Most notably in the book of Kings: 1 Kgs 3:2–4; 11:7; 12:31–32; 13:2, 32–33; 14:23; 15:14; 22:43; 2 Kgs 12:3; 14:4; 15:4, 35; 16:4; 17:9, 11, 29, 32; 18:4, 22; 21:3; 23:5, 8–9, 13, 15, 19–20.

42. Judg 5:5; Ps 18:7(8); Hab 3:6, 10.

43. See the Baal myth in COS 1.186:241–274. In this mythic tale Baal defeats Yam, which allows him to claim the right to build a palace in the sky, but when Baal fights Mot, he loses the battle so that he must descend into the netherworld instead of living with the other deities. This conceptualization of a three-tiered universe is a fundamental piece of the ancient Near Eastern worldview long before and long after the time of Micah. So, by itself, this motif cannot be used to date this text absolutely. One must look to the larger context.

44. Several recent redactional models have concluded that Mic 1:5 (and the opening verses with which it belonged) originally only pronounced judgment upon Samaria or upon Judah. Cf. Schart, Die Entstehung, 179–80; Lescow, “Redaktionsgeschichtliche Analyse von Micha 1–5,” 54, 63; and Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 140–42. Schart’s foundational layer in 1:2–7* includes 1:6–7, and he understands Samaria as the object of judgment. Schart considers 1:3–4 secondary, while Lescow and Wöhrle consider 1:3–4 to be integral. Lescow and Wöhrle, in contrast to Schart, argue that 1:5b–7 are insertions. For them, Samaria was not part of the original unit, but was only added later, during the exilic period. Lescow bases his argument on the fact that 1:10–16 deals with the events of Sennacherib’s siege, some two decades after Samaria’s destruction, while the core material of the first unit (1:3–5a, 8–9) relates integrally to 1:10–16. Wöhrle—like Lescow—considers 1:5b–7 as secondary, while Schart considers it part of the primary layer.

45. See esp. Jeremias, 134–35.

46. For a detailed explanation of the parallelism of this verse, see David Noel Freedman, “Discourse on Prophetic Discourse,” in The Quest for the Kingdom of God: Studies in Honor of George E. Mendenhall, ed. Herbert B. Huffmon (Winona Lake, IN: Eisenbrauns, 1983), 147.

47. Lescow, “Redaktionsgeschichtliche Analyse von Micha 1–5,” 64.

48. Schart, Die Entstehung, 178–81; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 141; Jeremias, 136. Schart and Wöhrle argue that the verses are best suited to the late exilic period while Jeremias sees the verses entering in two parts, with only 1:7a definitively coming from the exilic or early postexilic period.

49. For Schart, the later material adds to the compositional layer by incorporating Mic 1:1–2a, 5b into the compositional layer (1:2b, 5a, 6–8). The added material shows knowledge of Deuteronomistic traditions, and it is followed by a second insertion—the theophanic material in Mic 1:3–4 that mirrors the theophany of Amos and shows parallels with Zephaniah.

50. Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 275–77.

51. E.g., Wöhrle argues that 1:5b–7 was inserted as part of his Deuteronomistic layer (Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 139–41). For him, 1:2–16 constitutes a series of individual sayings (1:2, 3–4, 5–7, 8–9, 10–15, 16) and by eliminating 1:5b–7 as part of the core Wöhrle identifies Jacob/Israel in 1:5a as the target. He identifies Jacob/Israel as Judah because the phrase appears elsewhere in Micah (2:12; 3:1, 8, 9) where he considers the terms to refer to Judah. Nevertheless, without 1:6–7 (and its anti-idolatry polemic), the theophany (1:3–4) remains disconnected from any reason for judgment.

53. The same word is used in both verses, but 1:6 uses a singular form when referring to Samaria while 3:12 refers to “piles” in the plural.

56. Based upon the observations of Tyler Fulcher in an Old Testament Colloquium at Baylor University on 11 April 2022. 57. Johan Lust, Erik Eynikel, Katrin Hauspie, eds., Greek-English Lexicon of the Septuagint (Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 2003), s.v. “kenos,” 336–37. See also the ways in which prepositions appear more prominent in the Greek translations because they represent Hebrew idioms more literally, with eōs used for ʿal and eis used for the Hebrew l preposition.

59. See Schart, Die Entstehung, 180–83; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 142–46.

60. Schart, e.g., sees all of 1:2–7 as a composition written to join a layer of Joel that presupposes knowledge of the theology of Deuteronomy, which was composed after the finding of the book of the law in the time of Josiah in 622. See Schart, Die Entstehung, 177–81.

61. See Sweeney, 2:354. He argues intriguingly that the towns mentioned in 1:10–12 would have been in the vicinity of Gath, in the coastal plain. Sweeney sees these towns as part of the land taken by Hezekiah in preparation for his revolt against the Assyrians. By contrast, he thinks that the towns in 1:13–15 represent Judean cities of the Shephelah. Sennacherib, coming from the coast, would have taken the cities of the coastal plain to secure his position before taking his army uphill into Judah proper.

62. E.g., Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 144–45, 196–97; and Schart, Die Entstehung, 182–83. Wöhrle places 1:12b with his Deuteronomistic layer, but labels 1:13b as an isolated gloss because it does not use characteristically Deuteronomistic vocabulary. Schart also places 1:12b and 1:13b in different redactional layers since 1:13b takes up the vocabulary of 1:5 (sin, rebellion) to comment upon 1:13a. Both Wöhrle and Schart, then, see 1:12b, 13b as brief insertions designed to link 1:10–16 with 1:2–7. The subtle distinctions they make between two different layers, however, could also result from a single hand attempting to integrate 1:10–16 with 2–7.

63. See esp. Jeremias, 116. While noting this shift to the prophet’s self-reporting helps to follow the logic of the unit, it seems unwise to give so much weight to the fact that a prophet reports on his own behavior since such first-person accounts also appear in the seventh-century prophetic materials of Habakkuk (1:2; 2:1; 3:2, 16–19) and the fourth-century prophetic collection of Joel (1:19–20).

64. See Karl Budde, “Eine folgenschwere Redaktion des Zwölfprophetenbuchs,” ZAW 39 (1921): 218–29, DOI: 10.1515/zatw.1921.39.1.218; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 177–80; Mays, 54–56; and Jeremias, 116. For Wöhrle (178), this first-person prophetic speech even causes him to include 7:1–7 in his foundational layer of Micah, though almost every other scholar sees 7:1–7 as part of the postexilic expansions of the book.

66. See also the discussions of Mic 4:1–4 (= Isa 2:2–4) and the use of Isa 9–10 in Mic 7:8–20 in this commentary.

67. The work of Elliger, has been very influential in this respect. Karl Elliger, “Die Heimat des Propheten Micha,” ZDP 57 (1934): 81–152. See also Mays, 52–54; Rudolph, 50. Wolff (53–54) goes against the grain, by arguing that the attack refers to a time even earlier (733–723 BCE).

68. See Wolff, 58; and Allen, 275. Allen poignantly notes: “Micah abandons himself to banshee cries, sounding like the plaintive howl of the jackal at night or the gruesome screech of the ostrich.”

69. See Othmar Keel and Christoph Uehlinger, Gods, Goddesses, and Images of God in Ancient Israel, trans. Thomas H. Trapp (Minneapolis: Fortress, 1998), 367–72. The seventh century BCE saw a dramatic rise in astral symbols in cylinder seals, including the representation of a Judean moon deity. They probably represent both Egyptian and Assyrian influences over an extended period. Just as significantly, the dramatic rise of manufactured terra-cotta figurines in the form of naked goddesses in homes across Judah (normally in household settings) shows that at the very least, private religion looked considerably different than the official religion articulated and presupposed in biblical texts. It also fits well with prophetic condemnations that imply that the worship of other deities was rampant in the eighth and seventh centuries BCE.

70. For summary of the increased astral symbolism in the seventh century BCE, see Keel and Uehlinger, Gods, Goddesses, and Images of God, 367–72. This glyptic art begins to manifest astral motifs within the religious symbol system that dramatically changes from those of the previous century. These artifacts attest to increased Assyrian influence on the culture.

71. This passage represents a theological summary of the failure of the Northern Kingdom (2 Kgs 17:7–18) followed by a brief but poignant application of this condemnation of Israel to the actions of Judah (17:19–20).

72. E.g., Schart, Die Entstehung, 181–82; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 143. Both see the entire verse as a later insertion. No consensus has been reached, however, on whether an earlier version of 1:2–7 existed as an introduction to 1:8. See the discussion of the growth of the book of Micah in the introduction to this commentary. Nevertheless, a significant number of redactional studies have indicated that Mic 1:3–7 did not exist in its current form prior to the exilic period.
